To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

triglycerides are an independent risk factor for CVD, that elevated triglycerides are a marker of CVD risk that reflects IR, obesity, and T2DM, and that lifestyle and pharmacological interventions can lower triglycerides and reduce the risk of CVD.
triglyceride levels are an independent CVD risk factor and that the risk of CVD increases with the number of CVD risk factors, including elevated triglyceride and LDL-C levels.

elevated triglyceride and TRL levels are atherogenic and are associated with increased cardiovascular risk, that the atherogenic potential of TRLs may be more important in the pathogenesis of CVD than the direct effect of triglycerides per se, and that the risk associated with elevated triglyceride/TRL levels is not fully explained by the presence of other CVD risk factors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that triglycerides play in cardiovascular disease and how this role can be modified by diet and exercise.
the role of triglyceride in the evaluation and treatment of CVD and its risk factors.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of the development of atherosclerotic lesions in the coronary arteries and their progression to clinical events.

triglyceride levels are an important biomarker of CVD risk.
the association between elevated triglycerides and CVD is not only causal but also independent of other traditional risk factors.

The main takeaway from our work is that
triglycerides and TRLs are important risk factors for CVD that should be considered in the assessment and management of CVM risk.
elevated triglycerides are an independent CVD risk factor and should be considered in the assessment of overall risk, especially in the presence of other CVD risk factors.
triglyceride levels are an important CVD risk factor that should be incorporated in CVD risk assessment and management.
